description: We are students passionate about technology, programming, innovation, and problem-solving. We enjoy exploring new ideas and turning them into practical solutions. We're looking for creative and enthusiastic teammates with skills in coding, web development, UI/UX design, research, data analysis, or astronomy. Most importantly, we value teamwork, curiosity, and a willingness to learn.
summary:
SPHEREx Sky Explorer is a website that lets anyone explore real images of the sky taken by NASA's SPHEREx space telescope, with no special software or training. You enter a location in the sky, and the app finds the pictures SPHEREx has taken of that spot, shows them in the order they were captured, and plays them like a slideshow. Its Time Machine also lets you compare two dates by flicking between them or viewing them side by side. All images come from NASA's public science archive, and the app clearly labels real data versus sample data used for demonstrations. It is designed to show differences between observations, not to claim new discoveries.

LIMITATION: Searching the live NASA archive from the deployed website can be very slow, sometimes taking several minutes, because each search first queries the archive and then downloads every image separately. When the archive is busy, a search can run past the time limit and fail, so results don't always appear. To keep the site usable, a demo mode with clearly labelled sample data is always available, and repeat searches load quickly while their results are still saved.

That is about 195 words in total, with the limitation paragraph included. If you need the summary paragraph alone under 200, it is already about 110 words.
details:
What does it do, and how does it work?
SPHEREx Sky Explorer is a website that lets anyone explore real images from NASA's SPHEREx space telescope. You type in a position in the sky, and the app asks NASA's public archive (IRSA) for every SPHEREx image covering that spot, downloads small cutouts, checks them, and shows them in the order they were taken. The Time Machine lets you step through them, play them like a slideshow, and compare two dates by blinking between them or viewing them side by side. We tested it against the live archive with a real search of the galaxy M101.

What are the benefits?
SPHEREx data normally needs specialist tools and file formats. Our app lets students, teachers and curious people explore it in a browser in a few clicks, with nothing to install. Caching makes repeated searches fast.

What is the intended impact?
We want to make a large scientific dataset approachable and encourage more people to look at real space-telescope observations. The app clearly labels real archive data versus sample demo data, warns that different data releases may not be comparable in brightness, and makes no discovery claims.

What tools, languages, hardware and software did we use?

  • Languages: Python for archive access and data processing, and HTML, CSS and JavaScript for the website.
  • Libraries: Flask, astroquery, pyvo, astropy, numpy, Pillow and requests.
  • Data: NASA/IPAC Infrared Science Archive (DR1 and QR3 releases).
  • Setup: a standard Windows laptop with VS Code, tested with Python's unittest. No special hardware. We used an AI coding assistant (Claude) to help plan, write and debug the code.

How is it creative?
The Time Machine turns an archive search into something you can see and play with. The blink comparison is inspired by the blink comparators astronomers have used for about a century: flicking between two images of the same spot makes differences stand out. A clearly labelled demo mode keeps the app usable when the archive is slow or offline.

What factors did the team consider?

  • Data honesty: every record is labelled real or sample.
  • Calibration: the interface warns that releases and bands may differ.
  • Reliability: downloads retry, results are cached, and one failed image doesn't stop the rest.
  • Accuracy of claims: we make no unsupported claims about discoveries.
  • Simplicity: a lightweight stack that is easy to run and extend.
  • Testing: we fixed real problems found in live testing, such as a rejected archive query and a Windows file-path bug.
